style: calm, natural hesitations, like explaining to a friend
slides: Okay, so just before we get into content, language, paragraphs and arguments...
let's look at an example task, and a pretty high-level essay that answers it.
Here's the example task. Read it with me.
First, the background. Security officials want a national network of face-recognition cameras in public spaces.
What for? To identify people in real time, and to stop offences before, during and after they happen.
Supporters say it'll reduce crime in the areas they watch. Maybe even get rid of it completely.
And the people against it say it'll seriously hurt our privacy.
So up to here, that's the background. And now the question. It always comes last, in bold.
So you've got two jobs. Say what you think, and explain why.
Now, what's this issue really about? It puts two values, two rights, against each other.
On one side, the right to life and security.
On the other side, the right to privacy.
And we have to say which one we think should win here... and explain why.
Let's see what the essay looks like. We start with an opening paragraph that gives the background to the debate.
Recently, security officials have been working to set up a national network of face-recognition cameras in public spaces.
The cameras are meant to help catch offenders, and thus reduce, perhaps even eliminate, crime.
However, some people have come out strongly against this move, because of the harm to privacy.
In my opinion, these cameras should be installed, since their benefits to public safety are likely to outweigh the harm to privacy.
So what does the opening do? It gives the background. And most of it comes from the task itself.
So the content isn't tested so much in this paragraph. It's stuff the task already gave us.
But there's one content point that's really important. I already say my opinion at the end of the opening. I'm for the cameras.
Why? To keep a clear main idea. So the rater knows exactly what I'm going to argue.
And then of course, in the next paragraphs, I have to explain why.
Now, language is checked everywhere. In the opening too. No mistakes, and a bit of richness.
Look at phrases like these. Have come out strongly against. Are likely to outweigh. They're calm, precise, and hedged. Careful, not too strong.
But, like we'll learn, you shouldn't overdo it.
And keep one steady register. I mean, one level of language, the same all the way through. Don't jump from everyday chat to fancy words.
Now the first argument paragraph. My first reason for the cameras.
In my opinion, the cameras would create deterrence, which would lead to fewer offences in the monitored areas.
It's reasonable to assume there'd be a campaign and signs. And that raises awareness.
That awareness makes offenders think twice, because their chances of getting caught have gone up.
For example, since cameras were installed at traffic lights, fewer cars cross on a red light.
It's a similar situation, so it stands to reason the same would happen here.
The paragraph opens with a key sentence. In my opinion, plus my reason. Deterrence, which leads to fewer offences.
Now, that's an opinion, not a fact. So I have to explain why I think it's true.
And that's the development. Step by step. Cameras, a campaign, awareness, offenders think twice, fewer offences.
We'll learn that nothing is obvious. You have to explain every step, from the cameras all the way to the result.
And at the end, support. Up to here I explained with logic. Now I compare it to a similar case, the traffic-light cameras, to make it stronger.
Notice, this paragraph talks about one argument only. Deterrence.
We'll learn this rule. One argument per paragraph. Two points from the same field can share a paragraph, but only when together they serve one argument.
A different reason doesn't go in here. It gets its own paragraph, or you just choose your strongest ones.
And it flows clearly. Connectors like for example, and as a result, show how each sentence links to the next.
And look at the hedging. It is reasonable to assume. It stands to reason. Not, the cameras will certainly.
That's academic writing. Careful claims, not sweeping ones. And it's two different phrases for the same idea, too. That's richness.
By the way... think twice, in quotation marks. Some people say quotation marks are forbidden in academic writing.
That's not true. It's better to use them rarely, but you can, when it helps the content.
Here, the informal phrase says it simply and clearly. That's fine. But once in an essay. Not more.
Now the second argument paragraph. My second reason for the cameras.
In addition, I believe the cameras could make law enforcement considerably more efficient, and save resources.
The police could act during the offence, and also afterwards. Identify, locate, prove guilt.
This would probably save time, manpower and money. Because without cameras, officers would have to question passers-by, and search for other evidence.
And then an example. A suspect caught in the act. The footage helps prove he's guilty, and then he can't commit more offences.
Look at the hedging again. Could make law enforcement more efficient. Not, will make.
Why? Well, for two reasons.
One, academic style. That's language.
Two, critical thinking. Telling opinion apart from fact.
Could make things more efficient says, this is my view. Will make them more efficient says it's a fact... and that's something I can't really know.
So in my opinion, or I believe that, comes once, at the start of the key sentence. Inside the development I don't repeat it. Hedging words, like could, may, and is likely to, do that job.
Notice there are some higher phrases. Not merely. Which in turn. But the essay isn't full of dictionary words.
It's normal, simple, clear writing. Just not everyday chat... with a higher phrase here and there.
One more thing. The first paragraph looked at the issue from a security angle. Fewer offences, safer citizens.
The second one looks at it from an economic angle. Saving resources.
And that's part of what they rate. Critical thinking means looking at the issue from several perspectives.
And it's built the same way. First a logical explanation, then an example to support it.
